title: regulated-pilot-starter-phrasing-and-negotiation-notes
summary: Concise starter messaging, negotiation levers and a technical pilot checklist for regulated workloads considering Redwood Private / VPC. Focused on early sales and solutions conversations—language to use with CISOs, procurement and infra leads.
content:
Purpose and audience:
This note is a short, pragmatic playbook for reps and SEs running pilot conversations with regulated buyers (healthcare, fintech, government). It is intentionally skinny — copyable lines for email/slide snippets, reframed objections, and a one-page technical pilot checklist to accelerate procurement/POC signoff.

Core positioning (one-liners to use)
- Redwood Private gives you a single inference runtime you can run inside your network so you keep data flows, keys and audit logs under your control — while we keep the model serving optimised and operational.
- For customers with regulatory constraints, we move the control of data and telemetry (KMS, audit exports, network egress) into your environment so compliance artifacts remain owned by you.


Buyer personas & primary concerns
- CISO / InfoSec: data residency, auditability, vendor access, breach blast radius.
- Head of Infrastructure / Cloud Ops: deployment repeatability, upgrade windows, resource isolation, support SLAs.
- Legal / Procurement: contract language for data processing, incident timelines, liability boundaries.
- Product/Platform engineering: runtime performance, observability, rollback/fallback behaviour.

Common objections and recommended reframes (copy-paste friendly)
1) "We can’t allow a vendor control plane to see our payloads."
   - Reframe: "We recommend a customer-managed control interface — you host the control plane in your VPC so only your network and KMS can decrypt any metadata. We can operate a lightweight assist plane for automation but it only receives encrypted, anonymised health telemetry unless you opt in otherwise."
   - Tech detail to offer: offer a scriptable demo showing admin endpoints bound to customer subnet + a KMS-backed key policy demonstration.

2) "We need proof it won’t exfiltrate sensitive tokens/PII."
   - Reframe: "We ship an audit hook and read-only incident archive to your SIEM by default; during pilot we can configure token redaction and prefix stripping; we will also provide a signed attestation for the pilot environment configuration."

3) "We handle upgrades ourselves — we don’t want opaque vendor changes."
   - Reframe: "Customers can pin runtime and model versions; upgrades are opt-in and scheduled. We provide a canary rollout path and release notes mapped to behavioral tests so you can validate before switching traffic."

4) "How is this different from me self-hosting open-source runtimes?"
   - Reframe: "Self-hosting often means maintaining kernel selections, batching logic, cache lifecycle and perf regression detection — all of which are subtle, high-maintenance costs at production scale. Redwood packages those operational investments with predictable performance SLAs, rollback tooling, and a small ops surface so your team can focus on product features rather than inference plumbing."

Negotiation levers and commercial language to surface early
- Pilot scope: limit to discrete dataset or route, 4–8 weeks, defined success criteria (latency percentile, cost per 1k tokens, incident tolerance).
- Escrowed config: offer to include a snapshot of the deployed runbook and configuration in escrow with a neutral third party for the pilot term.
- Temporary tighter SLAs: during pilot offer elevated response times for critical incidents (e.g., 1 hour P1 during pilot) in exchange for a shorter contract trial.
- Audit window & log retention: propose a pilot retention window (30–90 days) with option to extend in contract.
- Shared risk pricing: capped pilot charges + consumption credit applied to first bill if procurement converts to reserved capacity.

Technical pilot checklist (one-page copyable)
- Environment and network:
  • VPC peering or private link configured (CIDR ranges, allowed ports).
  • Admin endpoints bound to customer subnet; no vendor public control endpoint unless explicitly allowed.
- Keys and secrets:
  • Customer KMS configured for model encryption and signing.
  • Secrets never written to shared vendor storage — confirm key policy logs.
- Data flow and logging:
  • Sample request flow diagram agreed and signed.
  • Audit log forwarding to customer SIEM (Syslog/Cloudwatch/BigQuery).
  • Token redaction rules applied and tested.
- Operational playbooks:
  • Incident escalation matrix and P1/P2 contacts.
  • Canary runbook for model or runtime upgrades.
  • Rollback and degraded-mode behavior defined (fallback model, reduced throughput).
- Validation and success metrics:
  • Latency P95/P99 targets by route.
  • Cost per token estimate baseline.
  • Quality acceptance test — small prompt set + fuzz test results threshold.

Competitor framing (short notes for call prep)
- Managed cloud AI providers (big public vendors): better for speed of trial but typically keep control plane and telemetry in their tenancy — emphasize Redwood’s private option where we move control into customer VPC and provide the same DX while minimizing vendor-visible artifacts.
- Self-hosted OSS runtimes: cheaper headline cost but higher ops burden; call out kernel/quantization maintenance, regression detection, and SRE overhead as hidden cost lines.
- On-prem inference vendors: some require lengthy hardware procurement cycles — pitch Redwood Private as a faster path (BYO or cloud-hosted VPC) with comparable isolation but turnkey runtime tuning.

Example short email to CISO (copyable)
Subject: Quick pilot proposal — private inference inside your VPC
Hi <Name>,
We’ve helped similar orgs run 6–8 week pilots where the inference control interface and keys were hosted in their VPC. During the pilot we lock upgrades, forward audit logs to your SIEM and provide a signed configuration attestation. If you’re open, we’ll share a short technical checklist and a proposed success metric set for review.
Best,
<Aisha>

Call prep checklist for SEs (5-minute read)
- Ask: Is vendor control plane allowed? If no, propose customer-managed control interface and show architecture diagram.
- Ask: Where do audit logs need to land? Offer SIEM connectors and sample retention windows.
- Ask: Procurement timeline and required attestation artifacts (SOC2, ISO, custom questionnaires).
- Show: pinned model/versioning UI and canary workflow; demo switching traffic to fallback model.

Open questions and suggested next steps
- Create a short attestation template (one page) that legal can sign during pilot — SEs report it materially accelerates procurement.
- Build a small demo script that non-technical buyers can run: show a VPC-only admin endpoint, SIEM log landing, and a signed config exported.
- Collect three customer stories that quantify time saved vs self-hosting (Ops hours and incident count) to use in future pitches.

Notes on tone: be concrete, avoid absolutes. Regulated buyers react better to explicit guardrails (pinning, escrow, signatures) than to marketing promises. If you offer a temporary relaxation (e.g., vendor assist plane for automation), require it be agreed in writing, time-boxed and auditable.

Appendix: quick glossary to reuse in slides
- Control interface: the API/console used to manage deployments, rollouts and routing (we recommend either customer-hosted or customer-kms-protected).
- Assist plane: a minimal, optional helper service run by Redwood that can perform non-sensitive automation tasks; it never receives plaintext payloads without explicit opt-in.
- Escrowed runbook: a snapshot of configuration, runbooks and scripts stored with a neutral third party for the pilot term.

End of note.
